blocks.text: The female reproductive system consists of the gonads (ovaries), oviducts, uterus and vagina; the oviducts, uterus and vagina are its accessory organs.

items: Ovaries: two oval ovaries, 3 to 5 cm long and 2 to 3 cm wide, one on each side of the uterus, produce egg cells (ova or oocytes) and hormones. Their functional units are tiny sacs, the ovarian follicles, which nurture immature eggs. In an adult, one ripening follicle releases its egg each month (ovulation), and the ruptured follicle becomes a glandular corpus luteum.

Oviducts (Fallopian or uterine tubes): two tubes from the ovaries to the uterus. The released ovum enters an oviduct and is moved towards the uterus by cilia of the lining. Fertilization takes place in the oviduct, and the zygote begins mitotic divisions there.

Uterus: a hollow muscular organ with a fundus (the rounded top above the openings of the oviducts), a body (the main part) and a cervix (the lower narrow part opening into the vagina). Its wall has an outer thin perimetrium, a thick middle myometrium of smooth muscle and an inner spongy endometrium with a basal layer, whose stem cells regenerate it, and a functional layer that thickens and is shed in each menstrual cycle; in pregnancy it thickens further, the embryo implants and its vascular spaces join to form the placenta, which supplies the embryo and foetus with oxygen and food.
Vagina: a thin-walled tube 8 to 10 cm long from the outside to the cervix; the passage for the birth of a baby and for menstrual flow.

blocks.alt: Anterior view of the female reproductive organs in section: the pear-shaped uterus with its domed fundus at the top and the uterus body around the central cavity, narrowing into the cervix and the vagina below; an oviduct (fallopian tube) curves out from each upper corner and ends in finger-like fimbriae beside an ovary, which is tied to the uterus by a ligament.

blocks.text: Egg production begins before birth: oogonia (2n) in the follicles divide by mitosis into primary oocytes (2n), which begin meiosis I but stop in prophase I and stay there through childhood, for at least 10 to 14 years. At birth the ovaries hold some 2 million follicles, each with a primary oocyte. From puberty, one primary oocyte at a time resumes meiosis I and forms two unequal haploid cells: a large secondary oocyte (1n) and a small first polar body (1n). The secondary oocyte stops in metaphase II and is released at ovulation. If it is not fertilized it dies; if a sperm fuses with it, it quickly completes meiosis II in the oviduct, forming one large ovum (1n) and a small second polar body (1n).

blocks.alt: Vertical sequence with time bands. Before birth: oogonium (2n), mitosis, primary oocyte (2n) arrested in meiosis-I. Band: childhood, ovary inactive. From puberty to menopause: primary oocyte (2n), meiosis-I gives a first polar body (n, dies) and a secondary oocyte (n) arrested in metaphase-II; the secondary oocyte is ovulated and met by a sperm; meiosis-II is completed if fertilized, giving a second polar body (n, dies) and the zygote (2n).
